cl_xc_coping_during.q: What helps people get through a difficult trip?
cl_xc_coping_during.short: People most often said letting go, calming the mind, or lying down helped.
cl_xc_coping_during.but: This is what people remembered; no study tested whether any of it works.
how: In an online survey, 529 people who had had a difficult trip said, looking back, which of 26 things they had tried and found helpful.
About 85 in 100 named letting go or accepting it, 77 watching their thoughts without fighting them, and 74 closing their eyes or lying down.
In a US survey, trying to calm the mind was named most often, then moving somewhere else and asking a friend for help.
No study compared people who did these things with people who did not.

cl_xc_harm_reduction_habits.q: Do harm reduction habits mean fewer difficult trips?
cl_xc_harm_reduction_habits.short: In one small survey, people who recalled more safety habits had slightly easier first trips.
cl_xc_harm_reduction_habits.but: People remembered their habits and their trips at the same time, often years later.
how: 163 people who use psychedelics recalled their first and their latest trip, and which safety habits they had used.
More habits went with a slightly easier first trip than fewer habits, but not clearly with the latest one.
Most were with trusted friends; few tested their drugs, though testing was rated as important.
A review found almost no other studies of whether these habits work.

cl_alc_protective_strategies.q: Do habits meant to make drinking less harmful help?
cl_alc_protective_strategies.short: Students using more safety habits said they drank less, but whether the habits help is unknown.
cl_alc_protective_strategies.but: Most studies asked about habits and drinking at the same time. So they show links, not causes.
how: A 2013 review looked at 62 studies of college students.
In nearly every study, students who said they used more safety habits also said they drank less or had fewer problems.
Day by day, students drank more on days they had a sober driver or went home with a friend. The author thinks they planned these for heavy nights.
Students told to use more habits used more, but did not drink less (one study).

cl_benzo_own_practices.q: Do people's own habits lower the harms of benzos?
cl_benzo_own_practices.short: People describe staying home or having friends check on them. None of this has been tested.
cl_benzo_own_practices.but: No study compared people who do these things with people who do not, or measured harm.
how: A 2025 review found 35 reports on harm reduction for benzos.
On a Swedish drug forum, people wrote about staying at home, keeping the drug out of reach while high, and not drinking alcohol at the same time.
In Canada, some women and gender-diverse people who use drugs set up friend groups to check on each other.
After a test strip showed fentanyl, people in two studies said they took more care, such as having someone check on them. Harm itself was not measured.
